3 days ago - For about half a century, the discs were commonly made from shellac and these records typically ran at a rotational speed of 78 rpm, giving it the nickname "78s" ("seventy-eights"). After the 1940s, "vinyl" records made from polyvinyl chloride (PVC) became standard replacing the old 78s and remain so to this day; they have since been produced in various sizes and speeds, most commonly 7-inch discs played at 45 rpm (typically for singles, also called 45s ("forty-fives")), and 12-inch discs played at 33⅓ rpm (known as an LP, "long-playing records", typically for full-length albums) – the latter being the most prevalent format today.

s: A twelve inches, or 12" in short, is a vinyl record measuring 12 inches in diameter, i.e. 30.48 centimetres. This format is usually used for albums and more generally for the 33 rpm long play records, it is also used for the 45 and 33 rpm max or even some singles.
